results.title: TurboQuant Changes the Economics of Local AI Inference
results.content:
KV cache compression does not solve regulatory compliance by itself. It removes one of the primary technical reasons why regulated workloads end up in the cloud: memory constraints. The regulation provides the “why.” TurboQuant provides part of the “how.”

## Community Validation: Real Numbers, Not Marketing [...] Consider a compliance agent that reviews a 200-page vendor contract against internal policies and regulatory requirements. That agent needs 80K-120K tokens of context to hold the document, the policy database, and its own reasoning chain simultaneously. Without KV cache compression, that workload requires dedicated GPU infrastructure or a cloud API. With TurboQuant, it runs on a workstation under a desk. The agent’s context window is its working memory. KV cache compression keeps that working [...] The background: most enterprises run AI workloads in the cloud not because local models are worse, but because local hardware runs out of memory.   
A 100K-token context window for RAG over internal contracts and compliance documents consumes roughly 25 GB of VRAM in the KV cache alone.

results.title: Google’s TurboQuant: The Unsexy AI Breakthrough Worth Watching
results.content:
The KV cache is a temporary memory store that LLMs use during conversations. It keeps track of all previous turns in a chat so the model can maintain context. When you have a long conversation with ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, the KV cache grows with each message. This is why very long conversations can slow down or hit context limits. The KV cache consumes GPU memory, and compressing it means longer conversations on less hardware.

How could TurboQuant help small businesses running local AI? [...] What is Google TurboQuant?

TurboQuant is a compression algorithm developed by Google Research that reduces the memory footprint of large language models by up to 6x with zero accuracy loss. It compresses the key-value cache (the model's conversational memory) down to as few as 3 bits per number, enabling longer conversations and faster inference on less hardware. The paper was first published in April 2025 and will be formally presented at ICLR 2026.

Can I use TurboQuant today? [...] If you’ve ever had a long conversation with ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini and noticed things slowing down, or gotten a message that your context is too long, that’s the KV cache hitting its limit. We’ve all experienced compaction (compacting), which is another method to manage the cache by throwing away what you don’t need in a conversation. results.title: TurboQuant: What 3-Bit KV Caches Actually Mean for Your Inference Stack
results.content: TurboQuant (ICLR 2026, Google Research + NYU) compresses KV vectors down to 3-4 bits per coordinate with near-zero quality loss and no calibration step. The algorithm is a rotation and a table lookup. It runs online, meaning you quantize each vector the moment it is produced. No preprocessing pass over your dataset, no learned codebooks, no second-order statistics. For KV cache, that is the only kind of quantizer that makes practical sense, since vectors arrive one at a time during [...] The other systems-level benefit is simplicity. Methods like GPTQ and AWQ require offline calibration passes, Hessian computation, and per-model tuning. That works for weight quantization, where you quantize once and serve forever. For KV cache, the data is ephemeral and unique to each request. You need something that works on any vector, instantly, with no state. TurboQuant fits this constraint by design. Its codebook is precomputed from probability theory, not learned from data. Same codebook [...] The KV cache lives in HBM. During decode, the attention kernel reads it every single step. For each new token, you compute dot products between the query and every stored key, then weight the values. This is a memory-bound operation. The compute is cheap (just matrix-vector products), but you are bottlenecked by how fast you can stream key/value vectors from HBM into the compute units.

results.title: TurboQuant Compresses KV Cache by 5X. Does That Mean You Need Less Memory? | Everpure Blog
results.content:
### Summary

TurboQuant is a new compression algorithm from Google Research that delivers 5X KV cache compression with near-zero accuracy loss, freeing scarce GPU memory so LLMs can support longer contexts, more users, and bigger models on existing infrastructure.

image_pdfimage_print [...] Google Research dropped TurboQuant on March 24, and it compresses that cache down to 3 bits per coordinate with zero measurable accuracy loss. Not weight quantization. Not activation compression. The KV cache specifically, the thing that actually dominates your memory at inference time. I want to walk through the math in a way that’s easy to follow, then talk about what it means for your infrastructure.

## What did Google do that’s actually new here? [...] The KV cache is your browser with 300 tabs open. Each one made sense when you opened it, most of them you’ll never look at again, but they’re all eating RAM right now.

The model weights are fixed; they move in once and stay put. But the KV cache grows linearly with every token you process, and at long contexts, it becomes the thing that determines how many users you can serve, how long a conversation you can support, and whether your deployment fits on the hardware you already own.

results.title: Google’s TurboQuant Explained: How They Cut LLM Memory by 6x Without Losing Accuracy
results.content:
It’s wasteful.

Every time you send a long prompt, the model stores massive amounts of intermediate data in something called the KV cache. This cache grows with every token, quickly eating up GPU memory, slowing responses, and increasing cost.

Most solutions try to compress this memory, but there’s always a tradeoff. You either save memory or you lose accuracy.

Google’s TurboQuant breaks that tradeoff. [...] It compresses the KV cache by up to 6x and, in some cases, performs identically to the full-precision model.

That is a different kind of result. This article explains why, in plain English.

TurboQuant is a compression method that achieves a high reduction in model size with zero accuracy loss, making it ideal for supporting both key-value (KV) cache compression and vector search. It accomplishes this via two key steps: [...] Vector quantization is a powerful, classical data compression technique that reduces the size of high-dimensional vectors. This optimization addresses two critical facets of AI: it enhances vector search, the high-speed technology powering large-scale AI and search engines, by enabling faster similarity lookups; and it helps unclog key-value cache bottlenecks by reducing the size of key-value pairs, which enables faster similarity searches and lowers memory costs. However, traditional vector [...] Vectors are the fundamental way AI models understand and process information. Small vectors describe simple attributes, such as a point in a graph, while “high-dimensional” vectors capture complex information such as the features of an image, the meaning of a word, or the properties of a dataset.
